## Defect 1 — Webinar/retention: correlation treated as causation

**What's wrong:** The memo observes that webinar attendees have 31% higher retention among currently-active customers, then asserts "webinars therefore cause higher retention." No experiment or controlled comparison was done — attendees are self-selected. Customers who proactively sign up for and attend an optional onboarding webinar are plausibly more engaged, more organized, or more invested in the product from the start, independent of anything the webinar itself teaches. Engagement is a plausible common cause of both "attends webinar" and "stays subscribed."

**What it would cause:** Mandating webinar attendance for all new customers would force attendance on the disengaged customers who previously self-selected out — exactly the group whose retention the correlation says nothing about. If the effect is really driven by pre-existing engagement rather than webinar content, mandatory attendance could produce little or no retention lift while adding a cost/friction to onboarding, wasting the investment the memo recommends.

## Defect 2 — Sampling only currently-active customers (survivorship bias)

**What's wrong:** The 412 customers analyzed are those "still active on the Pro plan today" — i.e., the sample is filtered on the outcome (retention) before retention is measured. Churned customers, including any who attended webinars and churned anyway, are excluded entirely. This is selection on the dependent variable.

**What it would cause:** This can inflate, deflate, or entirely fabricate an apparent relationship between webinar attendance and retention, because the comparison never includes the customers who didn't retain. To validly test whether webinars predict retention, the analysis needs the full cohort of customers who ever started on Pro (attendees and non-attendees, retained and churned), not just survivors. As-is, the 31% figure cannot be trusted even as a plain correlation, let alone as grounds for a causal policy change.

## Defect 3 — Multiple comparisons / p-hacking on the region finding

**What's wrong:** Eighteen attributes were tested against churn, and one (Central region) came back significant at p = 0.04. With 18 independent tests at the conventional α = 0.05 threshold, the expected number of false positives by chance alone is roughly 18 × 0.05 ≈ 0.9 — i.e., finding "significant" one is exactly what you'd expect even if none of the attributes actually matter. A p-value of 0.04 on one out of 18 tests does not clear a corrected significance bar (e.g., Bonferroni would require p < 0.05/18 ≈ 0.0028).

**What it would cause:** Reallocating next quarter's spend to the Central region on the strength of this single uncorrected test risks chasing statistical noise. If the effect doesn't replicate, the reallocation produces no churn benefit and diverts spend away from regions/segments that may matter more.

## Defect 4 — Satisfaction increase: no significance/uncertainty check, and causal attribution without ruling out other explanations

**What's wrong:** A rise from 62% to 66% is reported as evidence that "the new support model is working," with no indication of sample size, confidence interval, or normal quarter-to-quarter variance in this metric. A 4-point move could be within ordinary noise. Separately, even if the move is real, nothing rules out other things that changed that quarter (seasonality, pricing, product changes, macro conditions) — the new support model is only one candidate explanation, and it's asserted as the cause without any comparison (e.g., no control group, no isolation of the support-model change from other concurrent changes).

**What it would cause:** Crediting the support model could lead to over-investing in or expanding that specific initiative while the true driver (if any) goes unrecognized — and if the 4-point move is just noise, the "improvement" may not even persist next quarter, undermining whatever decision was based on it.

---

No other defects found — the description says the underlying numbers themselves are accurate, so I've focused only on whether the stated conclusions logically follow from them.
